common_name: Pathfinder Switchgrass (Synthetic Nebraska Upland Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Pathfinder is a synthetic upland cultivar developed at the University of Nebraska from several native prairie parent lines and released in 1966.

directions: Pathfinder was bred at the University of Nebraska by intercrossing several superior upland switchgrass accessions, combining strong winter hardiness with improved forage and seed yield over the wild ecotypes it descends from. In the garden it behaves as a tough, leafy, upright switchgrass, holding blue-green color through summer heat and drought before turning warm gold-tan in fall, with fine seed panicles that catch backlight beautifully. It has a long history in Midwest conservation seedings and pastures, so it establishes readily from division and needs little more than full sun and a well-drained site. Cut back the standing winter clump in late winter before new shoots appear.

common_name: Summer Switchgrass (Cold-Hardy Northern Plains Upland Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean to average, well-drained soil in full sun; Summer was selected from native South Dakota prairie stock for its combination of early maturity and strong cold hardiness in the northern Great Plains.

directions: Summer is one of the northernmost-adapted switchgrass releases in commerce, selected from South Dakota prairie remnants specifically for the short growing seasons and severe winters of the northern Plains and prairie provinces. It matures and sets seed earlier than most upland ecotypes, an advantage in gardens with a short frost-free window, while still forming the classic upright, fine-textured clump of blue-green summer foliage that fades to tan through fall and winter. Its exceptional winter hardiness makes it a reliable choice for zone 3 shelterbelt and meadow plantings where showier ornamental cultivars may struggle. Cut the dormant foliage back hard in late winter before new growth resumes.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Sunburst was released by the Big Flats Plant Materials Center in New York and is adapted to the shorter seasons and heavier soils of the Northeast.

directions: Sunburst is an upland switchgrass ecotype selected and released by USDA's Big Flats Plant Materials Center in New York specifically for reliable establishment and winter survival in Northeastern conservation plantings. It grows as a dense, upright clump of medium blue-green foliage, producing airy seed panicles in late summer that persist as a warm tan haze through much of the winter. Because it was bred for regional adaptation rather than ornamental novelty, it tends to be exceptionally tough and low-maintenance once established, tolerating poor, compacted, or seasonally wet soils better than many showier cultivars. Cut the standing winter clump back to a few inches before new growth emerges in spring.

common_name: Shawnee Switchgrass (High-Yield Midwest Biomass and Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Shawnee was developed at Purdue University from Trailblazer and Pathfinder parent lines and released for improved biomass yield in the Midwest.

directions: Shawnee is a Purdue University-bred synthetic switchgrass cultivar, combining the upland hardiness of Pathfinder and Trailblazer parentage with noticeably higher biomass and seed yield, a trait developed for bioenergy and forage trials but equally useful for gardeners wanting a large, fast-filling screening grass. It forms a tall, upright clump of blue-green summer foliage that turns warm gold-tan in fall, with abundant, diffuse seed panicles that make it a strong choice for naturalistic hedging or a backdrop planting in a prairie-style border. Its vigorous growth means it benefits from slightly more generous spacing than smaller-statured switchgrass cultivars. Cut the dormant clump back hard in late winter before new shoots emerge.

common_name: Caddo Switchgrass (Drought-Tough Southern Plains Conservation Grass)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Caddo was released by USDA-ARS from native stock near Woodward, Oklahoma, and is bred specifically for drought tolerance on the southern Great Plains.

directions: Caddo is a more recent USDA-ARS release selected from native switchgrass populations around Woodward, Oklahoma, and bred for improved seedling vigor and drought survival on the hot, dry southern Great Plains. It establishes into a dense, upright clump of fine blue-green foliage that tolerates extended dry spells with little visible stress, turning a warm russet-tan through fall and winter. Its southern-adapted upland parentage makes it a strong choice for xeric prairie-style plantings and roadside or slope stabilization in hot summer climates where northern switchgrass ecotypes can struggle. Cut the standing winter foliage back in late winter before new growth resumes.
sources: USDA-ARS Southern Plains Range Research Station

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Shelter was released by the Big Flats Plant Materials Center in New York for streambank stabilization and conservation buffer plantings in the Northeast.

directions: Shelter is a Northeast-adapted switchgrass release developed for streambank and buffer-strip stabilization, prized for a dense, fibrous root system that holds soil on slopes and along waterways where erosion is a concern. Above ground it forms an upright clump of medium blue-green foliage with airy summer seed panicles that mature to a soft tan by fall, providing food and cover for birds through winter. Its regional breeding for regional soils and rainfall patterns makes it a low-fuss choice for rain gardens, pond margins, and naturalized buffer plantings in the Northeast. Cut back the dormant clump in late winter before new shoots emerge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Grenville was released by the Los Lunas Plant Materials Center in New Mexico for revegetation of disturbed sites in the arid Southwest.

directions: Grenville was selected in New Mexico for use on disturbed rangeland, mine reclamation sites, and roadcuts across the arid Southwest, where reliable establishment under low rainfall matters more than the size or novelty prized in ornamental cultivars. It stays more compact than switchgrass ecotypes bred for wetter regions, forming a tight, upright clump of gray-green foliage that copes with intense sun and long dry spells with minimal irrigation once established. In a garden setting it works well as a tough, water-thrifty structural grass for xeriscapes and high-plains prairie-style plantings, coloring warm tan through fall and winter. Cut the dormant clump back in late winter before new growth begins.

planting.note: Start transplants or plant container-grown divisions in spring in sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; Atlantic was released by the Cape May Plant Materials Center in New Jersey for dune and beachfront stabilization along the mid-Atlantic coast.

directions: Atlantic coastal panicgrass was released specifically for dune building and beachfront revegetation along the mid-Atlantic seaboard, selected for vigorous rhizome spread and a deep root system that traps blowing sand and rebuilds dune profiles after storm damage. It forms an upright clump of coarse, blue-green foliage topped by open, diffuse seed panicles in late summer, tolerating salt spray, sandy infertile soil, and drought far better than most garden grasses. In coastal landscapes it pairs naturally with sea oats and American beachgrass for erosion control, or works as a tough, low-maintenance specimen in inland gardens with hot, sandy sites. Cut back the winter foliage in late winter before new growth resumes.

common_name: Little Nicky Miscanthus (Compact Variegated Maiden Grass)

planting.note: Plant container divisions in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; Little Nicky (sold under the cultivar name 'Hinjo') is a patented dwarf variegated selection bred for smaller gardens and container use.

directions: Little Nicky is a compact, patented Miscanthus selection marketed under the trade name Little Nicky for the cultivar 'Hinjo', bred to bring the fine-textured, white-edged look of larger maiden grasses down to a scale that fits patio containers and small borders. Narrow blades carry a crisp white margin around a green center, giving the clump a bright, luminous quality all season that intensifies as cooler fall weather sets in and the foliage picks up burgundy tones. It stays noticeably smaller and tighter than 'Little Zebra' or 'Adagio', reaching only about knee height, and rarely produces significant seed, which limits self-sowing compared to larger miscanthus cultivars. Cut the clump back to a few inches in late winter before new shoots emerge, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.
